statement: Tap A alone fills a tank in 6 hours, and tap B alone fills it in 3 hours. A drain alone empties the full tank in 4 hours. The tank starts empty, and both taps and the drain are opened together. How long does it take to fill the tank?

choices.misconception: I added the drain's rate instead of subtracting it, getting 3/4 of a tank per hour.
I ignored the drain and found how long the two taps take on their own.
I combined the times directly, 6 + 3 - 4, instead of combining the rates.
I simply added the three times 6, 3 and 4 together.

hints: What fraction of the tank does each one handle in one hour?
Times do not add, but rates do. Turn each time into a fraction of the tank per hour, give the drain a minus sign, combine, and turn the combined rate back into a time.
Per hour, tap A fills 1/6, tap B fills 1/3, and the drain removes 1/4 of the tank.

solutions.reliable: In one hour tap A fills 1/6 of the tank, tap B fills 1/3, and the drain empties 1/4. Together the tank gains 1/6 + 1/3 - 1/4 = 2/12 + 4/12 - 3/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 of a tank per hour, so it is full after 4 hours. The transferable idea: in work problems add rates, never times, and give opposing work a negative rate.
solutions.elegant: Imagine the tank holds 12 litres. Tap A gives 2 litres per hour, tap B gives 4, and the drain removes 3, so the tank gains 3 litres per hour and fills in 12 / 3 = 4 hours.

whyOnTest: Combined work rates test adding rates rather than times, and the drain checks that you give opposing work a negative sign.
